title: HIPAA Compliant AI Agents: A 2026 Requirements Guide
summary: HIPAA compliant AI agents rely on how you architect systems, not the tools. You'll identify the infrastructure and controls that determine compliance.
body_markdown:
## Build a compliant setup around the agent with Activepieces


**No workflow tool makes an agent compliant** , and Activepieces doesn't either; its MIT-licensed core lets a team inspect the controls around an agent and keep them inside its own boundary.


That layer matters because every connection an agent gets, to a records system, an inbox or a model provider, is a new liability line until someone has scoped it.


Look at the Agents dashboard to see what that scoping looks like in practice. Each agent is a named, listed object, here "Blog Author Enricher" and "SEO blog writer", sitting beside Flows, Tables, MCP and Connections in the sidebar.


For a reviewer, the point is that agents and the connections they use are managed in one place rather than scattered across personal accounts, which makes an inventory possible. An inventory is the precondition for every other control.


### Self-host to keep PHI in your environment


Activepieces runs self-hosted from its MIT-licensed core, including in an air-gapped setup, which keeps the workflow itself inside the team's own network.


For a regulated team, this is the practical route: the orchestration layer, its stored run data and its credentials stay in an environment the team already controls and audits.


The core is MIT-licensed, and the public GitHub repository (25,087 stars, 741 integrations in its community integrations directory) shows exactly what runs inside that boundary before anything is installed; its LICENSE file puts only the` packages/ee/` directories under a separate commercial licence.


You pay for it operationally. The team now owns patching, backups and uptime, which the managed cloud would otherwise carry.


If a team prefers not to run infrastructure, it can use the managed cloud in an EU or US region, which settles where data resides but not who operates the servers.


### Access control and audit trail


When someone leaves the company and is deprovisioned, their access to workflows and connections ends with it: Activepieces holds a SOC 2 Type II report and supports SSO and SCIM, so access follows the identity provider.


With custom RBAC, a team separates who builds a flow, who may use a connection holding patient records, and who may only view runs.


The enterprise RBAC documentation spells out that these access policies also apply to which connections an agent may use, so the agent sits inside the same access model as the staff around it.


Audit logs record what changed and who changed it, which is the evidence an assessor will ask for, and the run detail view for an agent step lists each tool call separately, with its own input and output.


### What it does not do


Do not look to Activepieces for a BAA: it doesn't offer one, and it doesn't claim HIPAA certification; the MIT-licensed core is something to inspect, not an agreement to sign.


The model provider the agent calls, and any other service in the chain, still needs its own agreement and its own review.


Self-hosting keeps the workflow layer in your environment; it doesn't cover a downstream vendor that receives the data. Minimum necessary PHI remains a design decision the team must make in each flow.
